strengths: The problem formulation is well-motivated and realistic: selecting auxiliary data from a large general corpus when no validation set or large in-domain pool exists, which genuinely breaks the assumptions of LESS/DSIR/TSDS-style methods. This is a clear and useful niche.

The empirical validation of 'NTK-like behavior' in LoRA fine-tuned LLMs (Frobenius cosine similarity >0.99 in Figure 2a, plus eNTK kernel regression recovering >90% of fine-tuning accuracy in Table 3) is a nice empirical contribution that grounds the method, going beyond simply borrowing the NTK formalism.

The Jacobian-free approximation (summing output gradients instead of the full Jacobian) combined with LoRA-restricted gradients and random projection is a practical, memory-efficient design, and the runtime/complexity analysis (Table 4, ~31h on one A100 for 1.8M candidates) makes the cost transparent.

Experiments are reasonably broad: 8 tasks across 4 domains, two backbone models (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), and multiple selection baselines (Random, DSIR, LESS, TSDS). Ablations cover pre-selection size M, projection dimension, auxiliary data scale, and target-data size (Figures 3-5, Tables 2-3).

Detailed appendices (proofs, kernel ridge regression derivation, full training hyperparameters, prompts, case studies of selected samples) support reproducibility, and the limitations of the eNTK regression experiments (medical tasks excluded) are honestly disclosed.
The finding that NTK-Selector is the only method that improves every task for Qwen3-8B, while other selectors sometimes catastrophically degrade performance, is a practically valuable observation.
weaknesses: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere. LoRA fine-tuning on 1K-10K samples is known to have substantial run-to-run variance, and several claimed improvements over the strongest baselines (e.g., 76.6 vs 74.8 for LESS/TSDS on Llama3; 78.6 vs 77.7 for DSIR on Qwen3-8B) are within the plausible noise range. This is the most serious evidential weakness for a paper whose central claim is that NTK-Selector is 'the only consistently effective approach'.

The headline '10.9x and 5.7x improvement' framing is misleading: it is a ratio against a nearly zero baseline gain (+0.8/+0.9 points from domain-only fine-tuning). The absolute gains (+8.7/+5.1) are meaningful, but the multiplicative framing inflates the contribution, and the margin over strong baselines (Random already reaches 74.3 on Llama3) is much smaller.

A critical ablation is missing: the method is a two-stage pipeline where embedding-based pre-selection (S_pre) does the heavy lifting of reducing 1.8M candidates to M=4N. There is no 'random selection within S_pre' or 'embedding-similarity-only (no NTK scoring)' baseline, so the marginal contribution of the NTK utility score over a well-executed nearest-neighbor pre-selection is not isolated. Table 2 varies M but never removes the NTK stage.

The NTK-like behavior evidence (Figure 2a) is only demonstrated on one task (financial sentiment analysis). It is unclear whether the directional stability of the kernel holds across domains with very different structure (e.g., document-level NLI with 3K-token contracts), which weakens the generality of the theoretical grounding.

Some baseline results look pathological rather than informative: LESS dropping 49.8 points on FPB for Qwen3-8B (30.3 vs 80.1 base) suggests implementation/configuration problems, not a fair reflection of the method, which complicates the 'only consistent method' narrative.

Theorem 1 is a fairly direct consequence of projecting the time-varying kernel onto the initial kernel plus a time reparameterization; the bound is loose and epsilon is never measured or quantified in practice. Relatedly, the 'first systematic study of kernel behavior in LLMs' claim somewhat overstates novelty relative to Malladi et al. (2023) and Wei et al. (2022), which the paper itself cites and builds on.

The greedy top-N selection by utility score ignores diversity among selected auxiliary samples; prior gradient-based selection work (e.g., TagCoS, cited in the related work) addresses this, and no comparison or discussion of redundancy is provided.

Training data quality is confounded by GPT-4o-mini-generated chain-of-thought responses, and the 'TAIA evaluation strategy' is adopted for some settings; these choices add hyperparameters/decisions that could affect comparisons but are not ablated.

strengths: The problem setting is realistic and well-motivated: selecting auxiliary data from a large general corpus when neither a large in-domain pool nor a validation set exists, which is a genuine gap relative to LESS/DSIR/TSDS-style methods.

Empirical evaluation is broad in scope: two backbone models (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), four low-resource domains spanning eight tasks, several selection baselines, and multiple ablations (auxiliary-data scaling, target-set size, projection dimension, pre-selection size M).

The paper does not only report end-task numbers; it includes supporting analyses such as eNTK kernel regression comparison (Table 3), runtime/complexity breakdown (Table 4), and qualitative case studies of selected auxiliary samples (Appendix A.8), which helps connect the method to its stated rationale.

Honest reporting of negative results in the ecosystem, e.g., that domain-only fine-tuning can degrade performance and that random augmentation sometimes hurts stronger models (Qwen3-8B), is useful context for practitioners.
Theorem 1 and the Jacobian-free approximation are clearly stated, with proofs in the appendix, and the Frobenius cosine similarity framing (Definition 1) is a concrete, testable formalization.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 is essentially a least-squares decomposition plus a time reparameterization; the resulting perturbation bound uses loose norm inequalities (spectral ≤ Frobenius) and does not itself justify the data-selection score. The claim of being the 'first' systematic study of kernel behavior in LLMs under instruction tuning overstates novelty relative to Malladi et al. (2023) and Wei et al. (2022), which the paper itself cites.

A critical ablation is missing: the two-stage design conflates embedding-based pre-selection with NTK scoring, but there is no baseline that simply takes the top-N samples by embedding similarity (i.e., skipping the NTK stage entirely). Without this, it is unclear how much of the gain is attributable to the NTK machinery versus cheap semantic nearest-neighbor retrieval, which is the paper's central claim.

Evidence for the core 'NTK-like behavior' assumption is narrow: Figure 2a shows kernel stability only for the financial sentiment analysis task and two models, yet this assumption is relied upon globally across four heterogeneous domains. The cross-term analysis for the Jacobian-free approximation (≈6% of exact NTK) is likewise empirical, on a limited setting.

Statistical rigor is lacking. All results appear to be single runs with no error bars, confidence intervals, or seed variance, despite several headline margins being small (e.g., 76.6 vs. 74.8 for LESS/TSDS on Llama3; MMLU-Med +0.4 for Qwen3), and 1K domain samples being randomly drawn. Conclusions of 'consistent improvement' are not statistically supported.

Baseline comparability is questionable. LESS requires a validation set that the problem setting forbids; the adaptation (warm-up on 0.1% of candidate data, mixed Adam/SGD gradients) deviates substantially from its original design, so the severe LESS failure (a 49.8-point drop on FPB for Qwen3-8B) may reflect implementation mismatch rather than a property of influence-function selection. Similarly, the asymmetric adoption of the TAIA evaluation strategy for medical/legal mixed-training runs introduces an evaluation-protocol confound.

Attribution of gains is muddied by GPT-4o-mini-generated chain-of-thought responses being injected into the training data; the interplay between synthetic CoT augmentation and the selection method is not disentangled.

Potential leakage concern in the eNTK regression analysis: the regularization parameter λ is 'determined through a hyperparameter search,' but the selection criterion (validation vs. test) is unspecified; given the no-validation-set premise, if test accuracy was used this weakens the Table 3 evidence.

Practical cost is significant (~31 A100-hours per selection) and is only partly justified; the paper's own diminishing-returns analysis suggests much of the benefit accrues at small scale, again raising the question of whether a much cheaper embedding-based alternative would suffice.

Reproducibility support is limited: a reproducibility statement lists appendix descriptions, but no code or data release is mentioned, and several implementation details (e.g., how Pi dimension 8192 interacts with LoRA gradient dimensionality, exact NTK ground-truth computation for Figure 2b) are underspecified.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: selecting auxiliary data from a large general corpus for low-resource domains without validation sets or large in-domain pools, a setting where established methods like LESS and TSDS are not directly applicable.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 8 tasks across 4 domains, 2 model families (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), and multiple strong baselines (Random, DSIR, LESS, TSDS), with consistent (if sometimes modest) gains for NTK-Selector.

Useful supporting analyses: scaling behavior with auxiliary data volume, sensitivity to target-set size, pre-selection size M, projection dimension, wall-clock runtime breakdown (Table 4), and an eNTK kernel-regression validation (Table 3) that lends credibility to the NTK-like hypothesis.

The paper is honest about weaknesses of auxiliary-data approaches (e.g., random selection degrading Qwen3-8B, LESS causing a 49.8-point drop on FPB), and the finding that NTK-Selector is the only consistently non-harmful method is practically relevant.

Theorem 1 and the Jacobian-free derivation are clearly stated with proofs in the appendix, and the two-stage design (embedding pre-selection + NTK scoring with LoRA gradients and random projection) is a sensible, practical engineering solution.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the core technical ingredients. The 'Jacobian-free approximation' in Eq. (5) is essentially the standard empirical-NTK trick of taking the gradient of the summed output (already used in e.g. Malladi et al. 2023 and Wei et al. 2022, which the paper cites), and random projection of gradients is standard in LESS/TRAK. The claim of being 'the first work to empirically investigate the kernel behavior of LLMs in the fine-tuning regime' overstates novelty relative to this prior line of work.

A critical ablation is missing: the paper never compares the full NTK-Selector against using only the embedding-based pre-selection stage (i.e., KNN-selected samples without NTK scoring). Without this, it is hard to attribute the observed gains to the NTK machinery rather than to better retrieval; Table 2 only varies M, not the selection signal itself.

No variance reporting or significance testing. The margin over the best baselines (DSIR/TSDS) on average is ~1.8-3.6 points, and Random already captures most of the gain over Domain-Only (e.g., 74.3 vs 76.6 on Llama3). Single-run results without error bars make these margins difficult to interpret, especially given the noted training instability in low-data regimes.

The empirical support for NTK-like behavior (Fig. 2a, cosine similarity > 0.99) is shown for only one task (financial sentiment) on two models; generalizing this to a method-wide justification requires broader evidence, particularly since the NTK is used to select data for very different domains (medical, legal, psychological).

Potential confounds and fairness concerns: GPT-4o-mini-generated CoT responses are injected into training data, and the TAIA evaluation strategy is applied selectively for medical/legal tasks under mixed training, which could differentially affect methods; the exact protocol for when TAIA is applied deserves more justification.

Possible leakage concern: the candidate pool (CoT Collection) may contain samples closely related to evaluation tasks; the Random baseline's large gains on RSDD (+16.6) raise the question of how much of the improvement is data volume/distribution matching rather than NTK-based selection quality.

Theoretical contribution is thin: Theorem 1 is a straightforward decomposition plus time reparameterization with a loose perturbation bound, and it is not clear the bound is ever empirically informative (ϵ is never quantified for the actual models).

Minor inconsistencies undermine polish: the abstract reports +5.1 points for Qwen3-8B while Section 5.2 reports 5.3; Eq. (5) has inconsistent notation (f(x; θ) vs f(x′, θ)); the NTK utility score is a plain average with no diversity mechanism, which is a fairly crude surrogate for the bi-level objective in Eq. (1).
Reproducibility is only partially addressed: the statement promises appendices, but no code or data release is mentioned, despite the method's practical orientation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: selecting auxiliary data from large general-domain corpora (CoT Collection) to improve low-resource domain adaptation, where existing task-specific selection methods (LESS, DSIR, TSDS) rely on assumptions (large in-domain pools, validation sets) that do not hold.

The empirical claim of 'NTK-like behavior' in LLM fine-tuning is supported by a substantial body of evidence: kernel cosine similarity across 10-50 epochs, multiple models (Llama3, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Hermes3), multiple fine-tuning strategies (LoRA, IA3, full fine-tuning), and hyperparameter sweeps (Appendix H.1), plus an eNTK kernel-regression sanity check (Table 3) showing kernel analogs achieve >90% of fine-tuning accuracy.

The theory is more careful than typical for this area: Theorem 3.2 provides a time-reparameterization argument bounding the perturbation from using the initial kernel, and Appendix E gives a genuine high-dimensional analysis of cross-output terms (bulk + low-rank Jacobian structure) extending Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022), with the assumptions honestly framed as 'high-dimensional regularity hypotheses' rather than exact claims.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: 8 tasks across 4 domains, 2 backbone models, 3 runs averaged, many selection baselines, compute-matched comparison against domain-only training (Table 12, addressing the 10x-data confounding), warm-up ablation (Table 13), overlap/leakage analysis (Table 14), extra genuinely low-resource tasks (Table 16), and clear runtime/storage analysis (Tables 4, 11).

Honest and nuanced reporting: the paper openly presents cases where auxiliary data or advanced baselines degrade performance (e.g., LESS's 49.8-point drop on FPB for Qwen3-8B, random selection harming Qwen3), discusses saturation/diminishing returns, and notes in the appendix that the warm-up stage contributes little.

Good reproducibility: detailed LoRA hyperparameters (Table 5), baseline implementations with links and recommended settings, evaluation protocol (CoT evaluation, vLLM, TAIA), and per-stage wall-clock costs.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the 'Jacobian-free NTK approximation' (Eq. 5) is acknowledged in Appendix E to be 'exactly a rescaled version of the pNTK' of Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022); the adaptation-side contributions (LoRA gradients + random projection + two-stage filtering) are standard engineering. The core selection score is essentially average gradient similarity, and its margin over the plain 'Gradient' baseline (76.6 vs 73.9 on Llama3; 78.6 vs 76.1 on Qwen3) and over DSIR (77.7 on Qwen3) is modest (~1-2 points average) and is reported without statistical significance tests despite 3-run averaging.

The headline '10.9x and 5.7x improvement over domain-only fine-tuning' is rhetorically misleading in the abstract/introduction since NTK-Selector trains on 10x more data; the fairer compute-matched comparison (Table 12) showing 76.6 vs 69.5 is relegated to the appendix.

The theoretical justification rests on strong and only heuristically motivated assumptions for a *trained* LLM: an isotropic Gaussian LM head (Assumption E.1) and a bulk-plus-low-rank backbone Jacobian Gram (Assumption E.2). The justifications (neural collapse arguments, outlier-dimension literature) are plausible but loose, and the resulting bounds are asymptotic in d; the theory therefore provides qualitative comfort rather than quantitative guarantees for the actual selection procedure.

The causal link between the NTK machinery and the observed gains is not fully isolated: the NTK component's advantage over pre-selection alone is shown (Table 15), but whether the specific NTK framing (vs. simply weighted gradient alignment at a warmed-up checkpoint) matters, and how sensitive the ranking is to kernel approximation error, is not deeply probed.

The 'low-resource' setting is partially weakened by heavy reliance on GPT-4o-mini to generate CoT rationales for domain training data, and on a 1.8M-sample curated candidate corpus; a truly data-scarce practitioner would need this extra pipeline, whose cost/quality implications are not fully analyzed.

Some presentational issues: the repository link is empty ('Official repository:'), Figure 1 and Table 1 numbers are slightly inconsistent, and the theoretical claims about kernel stability use a coarse scalar metric (Frobenius cosine similarity) that could miss meaningful spectral restructuring of the kernel.

The NTK-like behavior claim of 'first empirical evidence' for LLMs overstates the gap relative to prior work (Malladi et al. 2023, Afzal et al. 2024), which already examined kernel views of (smaller) LM fine-tuning; the contribution is primarily a scaling-up and systematization.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant and well-motivated problem: low-resource domain adaptation where in-domain data and validation sets are scarce, and the idea of mining auxiliary data from general-domain corpora is a sensible paradigm.

The empirical evaluation is broad and thorough: two model families, four domains (8 tasks in the main table plus additional tasks in Appendix H.11), many competitive baselines (DSIR, LESS, TSDS, embedding/gradient similarity), and useful ablations on pre-selection size, projection dimension, target data volume, and scaling behavior.

The authors address several important confounds: a compute-matched comparison against domain-only fine-tuning (Table 12), an ablation removing the warm-up stage (Table 13), and a documented-overlap check between the CoT Collection and test sets (Table 14).

The paper is transparent about limitations of the NTK framework for pretrained LLMs and provides extensive appendices covering the derivation of the approximation, kernel-regression validation, runtime analysis, and prompt templates, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The 'Jacobian-free NTK approximation' is, by the authors' own admission in Appendix E.1, 'exactly a rescaled version of the pNTK' of Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022). The remaining contributions (LoRA-restricted gradients, random projections, embedding-based pre-selection) are standard engineering choices, making the overall method largely an application of known components to a new setting. The framing of 'going beyond Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022)' oversells this.

The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 3.2 is a straightforward linear-algebraic decomposition (projection of the evolved kernel onto the initial kernel plus a time reparameterization), and the perturbation bound depends on the reparameterized time axis in a way that makes the practical significance unclear. The analysis in Appendix E rests on an 'isotropic LM head' assumption (E.1) that is plainly false for real pretrained LLMs; the justification via Neural-Collapse analogies is hand-wavy, and the final bound (Eq. 46) is heuristic rather than a rigorous statement about the actual models.

The core empirical observation (Frobenius cosine similarity of the NTK > 0.99 during fine-tuning) is arguably unsurprising: LoRA fine-tuning with moderate learning rates is a small perturbation of pretrained weights, so near-constancy of the kernel is almost expected. The paper does not demonstrate why this observation is surprising or what it rules out.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the claims made. Results are 'averaged over 3 runs' but standard deviations and significance tests are not reported for the main results. The headline advantage over strong baselines is often only 1-2 average points (e.g., 76.6 vs. 74.8 for LESS/TSDS and 74.7 for DSIR on Llama3-8B), and no confidence intervals are given to support 'consistently outperforms'.

Baseline fairness is questionable. The severe failures of baselines (e.g., LESS inducing a 49.8-point drop on FPB for Qwen3-8B) suggest possible misapplication of methods designed for different regimes (LESS normally uses validation gradients for a target task). The paper hypothesizes model sensitivity but provides no direct evidence for this explanation, and no sensitivity analysis of the baselines' key hyperparameters.

The pre-selection ablation (Table 15) shows 'Only NTK selection (M=|C|)' outperforms the default pipeline on all reported tasks, indicating the two-stage design trades quality for cost without a strong principled justification; the cost-quality tradeoff is discussed but the default M=4N leaves measurable gains on the table.

Presentation issues undermine polish: the first page contains an empty 'Official repository:' placeholder, and there are multiple typos (e.g., 'eactly' in H.2.2, 'β(x, xx)' in E.4, Table 12 header 'file * epoch').

The total selection cost (~31 GPU-hours per task-domain on an A100) is substantial relative to the scale of the problem (1K domain + 9K auxiliary samples), and the paper does not compare end-to-end cost against simpler baselines that achieve close performance (e.g., embedding selection at 74.9 vs. NTK-Selector at 76.6).

strengths: The paper addresses a realistic and well-motivated problem: low-resource domain adaptation where large in-domain data pools and validation sets are unavailable, and clearly frames why existing task-specific selection methods (LESS, DSIR, TSDS) do not directly apply.

The methodological core is reasonably principled: the paper empirically documents stable NTK-like behavior during LLM fine-tuning (Tables 6-8 across models, tasks, LoRA/IA3/full fine-tuning, hyperparameter regimes), provides a theorem (3.2) with proof bounding the perturbation under re-parameterized dynamics, and offers a theoretical justification of the Jacobian-free approximation via cross-output term analysis under explicit assumptions (Appendix E, with an O(d^-1/2 + sqrt(r)/d) relative error bound).

The experimental evaluation is broad and fairly thorough: 2 base models (Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), 8 tasks across 4 domains plus additional low-resource tasks (Table 16), 6 selection baselines, 3 runs, and many ablations (pre-selection size M, projection dimension p, target-data size, auxiliary-data scaling, warm-up removal, pipeline ablation).

Good experimental hygiene: compute-matched comparison against Domain-only (Table 12) rules out gains from extra optimization steps; 3-gram overlap analysis (Table 14) checks for test-set leakage from the candidate pool; eNTK regression (Table 3) independently validates the kernel-based view; runtime and storage are reported (Table 4, 11).

Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters (Table 5), baseline implementation details, prompt templates for CoT generation, and clear algorithmic description; CoT generation is shared across all methods, so it does not confound the comparison.
weaknesses: Margins over the strongest baselines are modest and not statistically tested: on Llama3-8B-Instruct the average is 76.6 vs 74.7-74.8 for DSIR/LESS/TSDS, and on Qwen3-8B 78.6 vs 77.7 for DSIR; per-task differences are sometimes within noise, yet no variance or significance analysis is reported for the main table despite 3 runs.

The central 'NTK-like behavior' claim rests on Frobenius cosine similarity of kernel matrices exceeding 0.99. This metric is dominated by the self-similarity (diagonal) structure of the kernel and may be insensitive to meaningful changes in cross-sample structure or kernel scale, so the evidence for 'stable NTK' is weaker than the 0.99 figure suggests; Theorem 3.2's perturbation bound also involves ||Theta_0||*||gamma||, making its practical tightness unclear.

The link from the NTK utility score (average kernel value to domain points) to the bi-level objective in Eq. (1) is heuristic: no theory or direct empirical evidence shows that maximizing this greedy score is near-optimal for downstream performance; the justification relies on intuition rather than a derivation.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the Jacobian-free approximation is essentially a rescaled pseudo-NTK from Mohamadi & Sutherland (2022) applied to LLMs (acknowledged in Appendix E), and the two-stage embedding-then-scoring pipeline is a common pattern; the main contributions are the empirical observations and the application setting.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix E relies on strong idealizations (isotropic Gaussian LM head, 'bulk + spikes' Jacobian Gram), which are argued plausibly but not verified for the actual checkpoints used; the authors are honest that these are regularity hypotheses, but the bounds are then only loosely connected to the empirical setting.

Some presentation inconsistencies: the abstract reports +8.7/+5.1 gains while the text reports +8.7/+5.3; the official repository field on page 1 is empty; the overall selection cost (~31 hours on an A100) is non-trivial for practitioners, though the paper discusses mitigations.

Reliance on GPT-4o-mini-generated CoT rationales introduces a dependency on synthetic data quality; the appendix argues this is shared across methods, but the sensitivity of results to rationale quality is not quantified.
